options.business_rationale: It limits answers to the provided material and shows where they come from.

options.text: A model that answers from its general training only
options.business_rationale: It wouldn't reflect the uploaded contracts.

options.text: A text-to-speech service
options.business_rationale: It reads text aloud but doesn't answer questions.

questions.scenario_question: A conglomerate's CIO has three requests: one team wants quick, no-code experimentation with agents over approved documents; another wants a production, governed, multi-model application; a third wants the strongest possible control by hosting an open model on its own hardware. Which allocation is the most sensible?
questions.hint: Match each request to its own maturity and control needs.

options.text: Open models for all three teams for uniformity
options.business_rationale: Uniform self-hosting burdens teams that don't need that control.

options.text: The developer platform for none, to avoid being locked in
options.business_rationale: That ignores platform advantages for governed production.

options.text: Low-code agent design for experiments.
options.business_rationale: Each request is matched to its level of customisation and operational responsibility.

options.text: Low-code agents for all three, including the governed production system
options.business_rationale: Production governance needs more than low-code experimentation.

questions.scenario_question: A hotel chain wants to give managers a daily summary of guest reviews, in structured topics and sentiment, from 30 languages. Volume is high; the output feeds a dashboard. Which approach is best to try first?
questions.hint: Structured tagging at scale in many languages.

options.text: Test both on a labeled multilingual sample
options.business_rationale: Real multilingual samples show which approach is best for structured output.

options.text: Only produce a poem summarising the sentiment each day
options.business_rationale: A poem isn't structured output.

options.text: Have staff read and tag reviews daily
options.business_rationale: It doesn't scale to this volume.

options.text: Use image generation to chart the reviews
options.business_rationale: Charts are drawn from the data, not generated by an image model.

questions.scenario_question: A solo founder wants to quickly test an AI chatbot idea over a few help pages, with no coding, to see if customers care. Which option is the most appropriate first step?
questions.hint: Prototype cheaply before investing.

options.text: Purchase a contact-centre platform for 10,000 seats
options.business_rationale: Over-scaled for an idea test.

options.text: Build a custom foundation model
options.business_rationale: Excessive for a first test.

options.text: A low-code agent design tool or managed search over the help pages, used as a prototype
options.business_rationale: It tests value fast with minimal investment.

options.text: Hire a research team to write a specification
options.business_rationale: Delays learning.

questions.scenario_question: A retailer wants product search that understands queries like 'gift for a gardener under 50 euros' and can recommend items. It has a catalog of 400,000 products. Which option is the best fit?
questions.hint: AI search and recommendations for commerce.

options.text: A workplace assistant for store employees
options.business_rationale: It targets staff, not shopper search.

options.text: A video model producing ads for each product
options.business_rationale: Ads don't improve search.

options.text: A speech-to-text API
options.business_rationale: It transcribes speech and doesn't rank products.

options.text: AI commerce search and recommendation capabilities built for retail catalogs
options.business_rationale: They interpret shopper intent and rank products.

questions.scenario_question: A bank must choose between a ready customer-engagement product and a custom conversational application built on the developer platform for its retail customers. The bank has few developers, standard use cases (balances, card controls, branch info), and a six-month window. What is the most defensible choice?
questions.hint: Standard needs and scarce developers favour configurable products.

options.text: Build a fully custom application, because custom is always superior
options.business_rationale: Custom is not always superior and costs more time.

options.text: Configure the ready product; customise proven gaps
options.business_rationale: It reaches value sooner with fewer developers while leaving room for customisation.

options.text: Do nothing until the bank has a large developer team
options.business_rationale: Waiting forgoes value.

options.text: Use a purpose-built translation API as the entire solution
options.business_rationale: It addresses only language conversion.

questions.scenario_question: A university wants researchers to experiment with a range of open and proprietary models for a study of summarisation quality, comparing them under the same conditions. Which option helps most?
questions.hint: A catalog and evaluation environment.

options.text: A built-in productivity assistant in the word processor
options.business_rationale: It is not a research comparison environment.

options.text: A text-to-speech service
options.business_rationale: It does not compare summarisation models.

options.text: A multi-model catalog with evaluation tooling
options.business_rationale: It supports controlled comparison across models.

options.text: A single fixed chatbot chosen by popularity
options.business_rationale: One model provides no comparison.

questions.scenario_question: A media company wants to automatically produce short branded video promos from scripts, with creative review before release. Which option is most relevant?
questions.hint: Generate video, keep review.

options.text: An image-only model, as video is just many still pictures
options.business_rationale: An image model doesn't produce coherent video.

options.text: Release directly to social media with no review
options.business_rationale: Unreviewed content risks brand and legal problems.

options.text: A speech-to-text API
options.business_rationale: It transcribes speech and doesn't create video.

options.text: A video model such as Veo, then creative review
options.business_rationale: It matches the output type and keeps accountable review.

questions.scenario_question: A ministry wants staff to find answers across policy circulars, regulations and past rulings, held in separate repositories with different access levels. Which factor should weigh most in picking an offering?
questions.hint: Access rights across repositories.

options.text: Whether the offering has a bigger parameter count than competitors
options.business_rationale: Size doesn't ensure access control.

options.text: Connectors that respect each user's access rights
options.business_rationale: Unified search must preserve the ministry's access boundaries.

options.text: Whether the offering can generate images
options.business_rationale: Images are irrelevant to the requirement.

options.text: Whether the offering has the catchiest name
options.business_rationale: Naming doesn't protect restricted rulings.

questions.scenario_question: A pharma company is deciding how to support regulatory submission writers who draft long, structured documents from approved source data. Quality, traceability and consistency matter most; volume is low. Which approach is the most defensible?
questions.hint: High stakes, low volume: quality and traceability first.

options.text: A governed drafting workflow using a capable model grounded in approved sources, with citations and mandatory expert review
options.business_rationale: It combines capability with traceability and accountability for high-stakes documents.

options.text: A free consumer chatbot used ad hoc by writers
options.business_rationale: It lacks controls and traceability.

options.text: The cheapest small model without grounding, because volume is low
options.business_rationale: Low volume reduces cost pressure, but weak grounding raises risk.

options.text: Fully automated submission writing with no expert involvement
options.business_rationale: Regulatory documents require qualified human accountability.

questions.scenario_question: A logistics company wants to reduce the time dispatchers spend answering routine driver questions by phone, such as parking, delivery windows and paperwork. The questions follow a stable pattern and answers live in a maintained knowledge base. Which option fits best?
questions.hint: Conversational self-service grounded in a knowledge base, with escalation.

options.text: A grounded agent that escalates exceptions
options.business_rationale: It automates routine questions and keeps people for exceptions.

options.text: A model fine-tuned to memorise the knowledge base, retrained when it changes
options.business_rationale: Retraining for changing content is inefficient compared with grounding.

options.text: A document extraction service
options.business_rationale: It doesn't hold conversations.

options.text: No automation, since drivers always prefer a human
options.business_rationale: That's an assumption, not evidence, and ignores a good automation case.

questions.scenario_question: A CIO must brief the board on how the company's AI portfolio should be organised. Which framing best reflects sound service selection?
questions.hint: Layers and personas, not a single product.

options.text: Let every business unit buy anything without coordination
options.business_rationale: Uncoordinated buying leads to duplication and weak governance.

options.text: Match each persona and need to its layer
options.business_rationale: A portfolio matches each persona and need with the right layer.

options.text: Decide each purchase by whichever vendor presented last
options.business_rationale: Recency of a demo is not criteria.

options.text: Standardise on one product and force every need into it
options.business_rationale: Forcing fit creates gaps or wasted cost.

questions.scenario_question: An HR coordinator asks a gen AI tool, 'Write something about our new leave policy.' The result is a generic, rambling paragraph. She needs a short announcement for all staff in a friendly but professional tone that covers three specific changes. What is the most effective first fix?
questions.hint: Tell the model the task, audience, tone, format and content.

options.text: Rewrite the prompt with audience, tone, length, and the three changes
options.business_rationale: Specific instructions and context are the cheapest, fastest improvement.

options.text: Switch to a much larger model, because vague requests are mainly a capability problem
options.business_rationale: A larger model can't guess unstated requirements. It may produce more fluent but equally generic text.

options.text: Tune a model on every HR announcement ever written, since style must be learned from examples first
options.business_rationale: Tuning is heavy for a one-off task that a clearer prompt can solve. It could help for a consistent house style at scale.

options.text: Raise the temperature so that the model produces something more original on its next try
options.business_rationale: Higher randomness adds variety, not relevance or accuracy to the three required changes.

questions.scenario_question: An insurer wants gen AI to classify incoming customer emails into eight categories and return them in a fixed label format. Zero-shot prompting gives sensible but inconsistent label wording. Which prompting technique is most likely to improve consistency?
questions.hint: Show the model what a good answer looks like.

options.text: Ask the model to be more careful and think harder without showing any examples
options.business_rationale: A generic request for care doesn't specify the labels. Models usually need to see the target format.

options.text: Add a few labeled examples of emails with the exact label format
options.business_rationale: Few-shot examples demonstrate the required pattern and wording.

options.text: Increase the output length limit so the model can explain each label in detail
options.business_rationale: Longer output won't make label wording consistent and may add noise to the classification.

options.text: Retrain the model from scratch on the insurer's mail archive until it learns the labels
options.business_rationale: Training from scratch is disproportionate and slow for a formatting problem.

questions.scenario_question: A law firm's associate wants a gen AI draft explaining a data-breach notification duty to a small-business client with no legal background. The first draft reads like a statute. Which prompt revision helps most?
questions.hint: Specify audience and purpose.

options.text: Add more legal citations to the prompt so that the model sounds authoritative
options.business_rationale: Citations raise formality, which is the opposite of what the client needs.

options.text: Remove all instructions so the model decides the style for itself
options.business_rationale: Fewer instructions generally produce less tailored output.

options.text: State the reader, their level, the goal, and ask for plain language with a short summary
options.business_rationale: Defining audience and purpose steers vocabulary and structure.

options.text: Ask for the answer in as many words as possible to cover all the details
options.business_rationale: Length without focus makes plain-language communication harder.

questions.scenario_question: A finance analyst asks a model to work out a multi-step revenue-recognition scenario and gets a confident but wrong single-line answer. Which prompting approach is most likely to help?
questions.hint: Encourage structured, stepwise reasoning, then check.

options.text: Trust the single-line answer because it was stated confidently
options.business_rationale: Confidence isn't correctness. Verification is needed.

options.text: Set the temperature to its highest value so the model explores alternatives
options.business_rationale: More randomness tends to reduce reliability on structured calculations.

options.text: Ask for a shorter answer so there is less room for mistakes
options.business_rationale: Brevity hides the reasoning and doesn't reduce errors.

options.text: Ask it to work step by step, state its assumptions, and show calculations to verify
options.business_rationale: Breaking down the problem improves reasoning, and visible steps make checking possible.

questions.scenario_question: An operations team feeds model output into a spreadsheet. The model's free-text answers sometimes include extra commentary that breaks the import. What is the best prompt-level fix?
questions.hint: Constrain the output format explicitly.

options.text: Manually clean each response before import for every single run
options.business_rationale: Manual cleaning doesn't scale and is error-prone.

options.text: Use a bigger model on the assumption that it will guess the import format
options.business_rationale: Models don't know the spreadsheet's requirements unless told.

options.text: Tell the model to write more elegantly so that commentary disappears
options.business_rationale: Elegance isn't format control.

options.text: Request a strict structured format such as JSON or a table, with no extra text
options.business_rationale: Explicit format instructions make output predictable for downstream tools.

questions.scenario_question: A marketing manager's first prompt for campaign slogans yields bland options. She has 30 minutes. Which approach is the most productive way to improve results?
questions.hint: Treat prompting as iterative.

options.text: Ask the model to rate its slogans and publish the top-rated one
options.business_rationale: Self-ratings don't replace human judgment on brand fit.

options.text: Commission a new model to be trained on competitor slogans
options.business_rationale: Training a model is slow and possibly legally risky for a 30-minute task.

options.text: Refine the prompt in rounds, adding brand voice, audience and examples, and compare outputs
options.business_rationale: Iteration with feedback quickly tunes results at almost no cost.

options.text: Accept the bland options since the model has done its best
options.business_rationale: The first output rarely reflects the best the tool can do.

questions.scenario_question: A retailer's support bot prompt says, 'Be helpful.' Testers coax it into offering unauthorised discounts. Which prompt-level control is the most appropriate first step?
questions.hint: Set boundaries in instructions, but don't rely on them alone.

options.text: Give the bot authority to approve any discount to maximise customer happiness
options.business_rationale: Unbounded authority is a business risk.

options.text: Add clear rules on what it may and may not offer, with escalation.
options.business_rationale: Instructions set boundaries, and controls outside the prompt enforce them.

options.text: Trust that 'Be helpful' implies the bot will follow company policy by itself
options.business_rationale: Vague goals leave policy gaps that users can exploit.

options.text: Remove the instructions entirely to avoid any chance of conflict
options.business_rationale: No instructions leave behaviour undefined.

questions.scenario_question: A pharma communications team wants summaries of an approved clinical document without the model adding outside claims. Which prompt instruction best supports this?
questions.hint: Constrain the model to the supplied text.

options.text: Instruct it to use only the provided document, quote key passages.
options.business_rationale: Constraints and 'I don't know' permission reduce fabricated additions.

options.text: Ask it to be creative and fill in any missing context from its own knowledge
options.business_rationale: Filling in gaps from general knowledge risks unapproved claims.

options.text: Tell it to summarise in as few words as possible, whatever is left out
options.business_rationale: Brevity at all costs may omit critical safety information.

options.text: Ask it to sound as confident as possible so readers trust the summary
options.business_rationale: Confidence encourages overreliance and doesn't improve accuracy.

questions.scenario_question: A consulting firm finds that every consultant writes their own prompts, with widely varying quality. Leaders want consistent, reusable results. What is the best organisational response?
questions.hint: Standardise and share what works.

options.text: Build a shared prompt library with tested templates, examples and guidance.
options.business_rationale: Shared, tested templates raise baseline quality.

options.text: Let each consultant keep private prompts and never share to protect competitive advantage
options.business_rationale: Siloed prompts duplicate effort and preserve poor ones.

options.text: Forbid prompts and require staff to write every document from scratch
options.business_rationale: That discards productivity gains.

options.text: Buy a bigger model and assume it fixes poor prompts
options.business_rationale: Prompt quality still matters with any model.

questions.scenario_question: A bank has two prompt versions for summarising loan files. A manager prefers Version B because it 'reads better.' What should the team do before adopting it?
questions.hint: Evaluate against criteria, not impressions.

options.text: Adopt B because managers' preferences are final for any prompt choice
options.business_rationale: Preference may favour style over accuracy.

options.text: Compare both on a test set against set criteria
options.business_rationale: Evidence on representative cases beats impressions.

options.text: Run each prompt once on a single easy file and choose the winner
options.business_rationale: One easy example can't distinguish quality.

options.text: Adopt whichever prompt is shorter, since short prompts are cheaper
options.business_rationale: Cost matters but not at the expense of accuracy.

options.text: Build a test set of real tickets, define criteria (accuracy, tone, safety), and have agents score outputs against them
options.business_rationale: Representative cases and clear criteria give meaningful evidence.

questions.scenario_question: A hospital evaluates a note-summarising tool using an automated overlap metric against reference summaries and gets a high score. Clinicians find that important allergy details are sometimes missing. What does this show?
questions.hint: Metrics can miss what matters.

options.text: Automated metrics may not capture clinical importance.
options.business_rationale: Evaluation needs criteria that reflect real risk.

options.text: Metrics should be removed and replaced by clinician opinion alone
options.business_rationale: Metrics still help at scale alongside review.

options.text: Evaluation is unnecessary because tools are always good
options.business_rationale: Evaluation is how problems are found.

options.text: The metric is reliable and clinicians are being too critical
options.business_rationale: Missing allergies matter more than overlap scores.

questions.scenario_question: A retailer's pilot assistant answers 85% of test questions correctly. The CFO asks if that is good. What is the most useful comparison?
questions.hint: Compare against the alternative you would otherwise use.

options.text: Compare with a competitor's marketing slide
options.business_rationale: Not a like-for-like comparison.

options.text: Compare with the current process or a simpler baseline on the same questions and weigh error severity
options.business_rationale: Value is relative to the baseline and the cost of mistakes.

options.text: 85% is always unacceptable
options.business_rationale: It might be fine for low-risk tasks.

options.text: 85% is always good enough in any context
options.business_rationale: Acceptable accuracy depends on risk.

questions.scenario_question: An engineering team tuned prompts repeatedly while checking the same 50 test questions, and scores climbed. The model then performed worse in production. What is the likely cause?
questions.hint: Overfitting to the evaluation set.

options.text: Production users are always harder than anyone can plan for
options.business_rationale: Not an explanation of the overfitting pattern.

options.text: The model was randomly worse in production
options.business_rationale: A systematic cause is more likely.

options.text: Prompts overfit the test set; use a fresh one
options.business_rationale: Repeated tuning on a fixed test set overstates performance.

options.text: The test set was too large
options.business_rationale: Large sets aren't the issue.

questions.scenario_question: A game studio plans a conversational character. Besides quality, what evaluation is essential before launching to a wide audience?
questions.hint: Safety and misuse testing.

options.text: No testing, as models are safe by default
options.business_rationale: Models can produce unsafe content.

options.text: Only checking that it greets players by name
options.business_rationale: Greeting doesn't test safety.

options.text: Only counting how many words per minute it can produce
options.business_rationale: Speed doesn't indicate safety.

options.text: Safety testing, including adversarial attempts to elicit harmful or inappropriate content, with monitoring after launch
options.business_rationale: Open-ended chat needs red-team testing and monitoring.

questions.scenario_question: A bank uses a second model to grade its assistant's answers at scale. A risk officer asks how much to trust the grader. What is the most balanced guidance?
questions.hint: Calibrate automated graders against humans.

options.text: Use the grader only on easy cases
options.business_rationale: That hides weak spots.

options.text: Trust the grader completely since it is also an AI
options.business_rationale: Graders can be wrong or biased.

options.text: Never use model graders for any purpose
options.business_rationale: They are useful when validated.

options.text: Calibrate the grader against human labels
options.business_rationale: Model graders scale but need calibration.

questions.scenario_question: A telecom firm's assistant scores well on accuracy tests, yet call-centre handling time hasn't improved. What does this suggest about evaluation?
questions.hint: Technical quality is not business value.

options.text: The assistant should be replaced by a larger one immediately
options.business_rationale: Cause unknown; investigate first.

options.text: Accuracy is the only metric that matters
options.business_rationale: Outcomes matter too.

options.text: Evaluation should include business outcomes such as handling time, resolution and satisfaction, not just answer accuracy
options.business_rationale: Good answers don't guarantee workflow improvement.

options.text: The call centre should stop measuring handling time
options.business_rationale: That ignores the outcome.

questions.scenario_question: A university wants to evaluate an essay-feedback assistant. Who should be involved in judging output quality?
questions.hint: People who know the domain.

options.text: Subject instructors using a clear rubric
options.business_rationale: Domain experts and rubrics produce meaningful judgments.

options.text: Random website visitors
options.business_rationale: Not qualified or controlled.

options.text: Only the software developers who built it
options.business_rationale: They may lack domain judgment.

options.text: No one; the assistant can judge itself
options.business_rationale: Self-judgement is unreliable.

questions.scenario_question: An insurer upgraded to a new model version and saw no complaints for a week. Months later, auditors found degraded accuracy on a rare claim type. What practice would have caught this sooner?
questions.hint: Regression tests and monitoring.

options.text: Testing only the most common claim type
options.business_rationale: That misses rare types.

options.text: A standing regression test set covering rare cases, run on every model change, plus ongoing monitoring
options.business_rationale: Changes can quietly affect niche cases.

options.text: Avoiding all model upgrades forever
options.business_rationale: Upgrades can bring benefits and are manageable with tests.

options.text: Waiting for customer complaints
options.business_rationale: Complaints are a late and incomplete signal.

questions.scenario_question: An e-commerce company wants to know if a new recommendation assistant increases sales. Which method gives the most reliable answer?
questions.hint: Controlled comparison.

options.text: Ask the sales team if they feel it helped
options.business_rationale: Opinion isn't measurement.

options.text: Count page views of the assistant's help page
options.business_rationale: Views aren't sales impact.

options.text: Compare this month's sales with last year's holiday season
options.business_rationale: Other factors confound the comparison.

options.text: A controlled experiment with a comparison group
options.business_rationale: Controlled tests isolate the assistant's effect.

questions.scenario_question: A logistics company wants to improve its dispatch assistant over time. Which feedback practice is most useful?
questions.hint: Capture structured signals tied to outcomes.

options.text: Retrain the model on every single message automatically
options.business_rationale: Uncontrolled training can degrade quality.

options.text: Ignore user corrections to keep the model stable
options.business_rationale: Corrections show where it fails.

options.text: Collect user ratings and corrections, review failures regularly, and add hard cases to the test set
options.business_rationale: Continuous feedback improves evaluation and quality.

options.text: Hide the feedback button to avoid complaints
options.business_rationale: That discards valuable signals.

questions.scenario_question: An insurer's broker-support assistant must answer questions about product rules that are updated every month, cite the exact rule, and keep answers in a consistent house format. The team has no labeled training set but has strong examples of the format. Which technique combination is most appropriate?
questions.hint: Each constraint points to a different lever.

options.text: Retrieve the current rules (RAG or grounding) and use a prompt with format examples
options.business_rationale: Fresh cited facts via retrieval and format via examples; tuning isn't needed.

options.text: Use only a longer prompt and no connection to the rules
options.business_rationale: Without access to the rules the model would guess.

options.text: Tune the model on the rule book monthly and skip retrieval
options.business_rationale: Monthly tuning is heavy and can't cite exact rules reliably.

options.text: Raise temperature so it adapts to rule updates
options.business_rationale: Randomness doesn't supply updated rules.

questions.scenario_question: A fashion retailer wants an assistant whose tone is unmistakably on-brand across thousands of daily replies. Prompting with guidelines helps but varies, and the brand team has 8,000 approved replies. Facts come from the product feed. Which approach should the team evaluate next?
questions.hint: Behavioural consistency with plentiful examples.

options.text: Use RAG alone for the brand voice
options.business_rationale: Retrieval doesn't impose a voice.

options.text: Tune on the approved replies for voice, and keep product facts coming from the feed
options.business_rationale: Tuning suits consistent voice; facts stay retrieved.

options.text: Tune the model to memorise the daily product feed
options.business_rationale: The feed changes; tuning would go stale.

options.text: Skip the approved replies and rely on a larger model
options.business_rationale: Size doesn't guarantee brand voice.

questions.scenario_question: A founder wants a first version of an FAQ assistant by the weekend. Content is a 20-page document. There is no training data. Which approach is the best starting point?
questions.hint: Start with the simplest technique.

options.text: Prompt the model with the document included, or use basic grounding, and test
options.business_rationale: A small document fits in context, so the simplest approach works first.

options.text: Build a large retrieval platform with custom ranking
options.business_rationale: Overbuilt for 20 pages.

options.text: Train a model from scratch
options.business_rationale: Disproportionate.

options.text: Fine-tune a model on the document
options.business_rationale: Needs data and time the founder lacks.

questions.scenario_question: A bank's compliance assistant must (1) answer from regulations updated weekly, (2) cite the clause, (3) refuse questions outside compliance, and (4) respond in a formal style. Which mapping of needs to techniques is most defensible?
questions.hint: Map each requirement to the right lever.

options.text: Tuning for all four requirements
options.business_rationale: Tuning doesn't keep weekly facts current.

options.text: Retrieval for all four requirements
options.business_rationale: Retrieval doesn't enforce refusal or style on its own.

options.text: Retrieval/grounding for (1) and (2), prompt rules and guardrails for (3), prompt examples or light tuning for (4)
options.business_rationale: Each technique handles what it's best at.

options.text: Higher temperature for all four requirements
options.business_rationale: Settings can't achieve these.

questions.scenario_question: A manufacturer is deciding the order in which to try improvements for its maintenance assistant: prompt design, retrieval over manuals, and tuning. Which sequence is generally sensible?
questions.hint: From cheapest and fastest to heaviest.

options.text: Change the model every week until results improve
options.business_rationale: Unstructured and unmeasured.

options.text: Prompt design, then retrieval, then tuning
options.business_rationale: Cheaper, reversible steps first.

options.text: Retrieval last, since manuals are rarely needed
options.business_rationale: Manuals are the key knowledge source.

options.text: Tuning first because it is the most advanced
options.business_rationale: Heavier steps first can waste effort.

questions.scenario_question: A law firm's assistant answers questions on a client's 40 contracts. Answers must reflect only those contracts and show where they came from. Which technique is the strongest match?
questions.hint: Private documents with citations.

options.text: Higher top-p to broaden answers
options.business_rationale: Broader sampling isn't retrieval.

options.text: Prompting with general legal knowledge only
options.business_rationale: That wouldn't reflect the client's contracts.

options.text: Tuning a model on the contracts so it remembers them
options.business_rationale: Less traceable and harder to update.

options.text: Retrieval/grounding over the 40 contracts with citations
options.business_rationale: It uses only supplied content and shows sources.

questions.scenario_question: A health-tech firm wants to improve a symptom-triage summariser that outputs variable structures. Facts come from the patient's note, which is supplied in the prompt. What is the most direct improvement?
questions.hint: Structure problem, not knowledge problem.

options.text: Retrain from scratch
options.business_rationale: Disproportionate.

options.text: Specify the output structure with examples in the prompt, and tune only if variation persists
options.business_rationale: The issue is format, which prompts address first.

options.text: Lower the number of patients
options.business_rationale: Not a technique.

options.text: Add retrieval from a medical encyclopaedia
options.business_rationale: The issue isn't missing knowledge.

questions.scenario_question: A media company debates RAG versus tuning for an archive assistant. The archive grows daily, editors want citations, and a small team will maintain it. A colleague says, 'Tuning is more advanced, so it must be better.' What is the best reply?
questions.hint: More sophisticated is not automatically better.

options.text: Disagree: tuning can never be used for media
options.business_rationale: Tuning has valid uses.

options.text: Agree: advanced techniques always win
options.business_rationale: No technique wins universally.

options.text: Agree: the team should hire more engineers first
options.business_rationale: Not a reason.

options.text: Not necessarily: with growing content, citation needs and a small team, retrieval is simpler to keep current and traceable
options.business_rationale: Fit to constraints decides.

questions.scenario_question: A telecom operator needs its assistant to adopt a specialised internal jargon used in network incident reports, which the base model misinterprets. The team has 6,000 labeled examples. Facts of current incidents come from a live system. What combination is best?
questions.hint: Behaviour from examples, facts from live data.

options.text: Ignore the jargon issue
options.business_rationale: It affects quality.

options.text: Prompt only with no examples
options.business_rationale: Prompt-only may not fix jargon mistakes.

options.text: Tune on labeled examples for jargon and style, and fetch live incident data through retrieval or tools
options.business_rationale: Tuning for behaviour, live access for facts.

options.text: Tune on current incidents each hour
options.business_rationale: Facts go stale instantly.

questions.scenario_question: A consultant's slide claims 'RAG eliminates hallucinations, so tuning is unnecessary and review can be dropped.' What is the best critique?
questions.hint: Both claims overstate.

options.text: RAG reduces but does not eliminate errors, and tuning serves different needs (style, behaviour), so review and technique choice still matter
options.business_rationale: The slide mixes up what each technique offers.

options.text: RAG increases hallucinations in all cases
options.business_rationale: Not generally true.

options.text: Tuning is always better than RAG
options.business_rationale: No universal winner.

options.text: The slide is right on all points
options.business_rationale: It overclaims.

questions.scenario_question: A retailer's AI steering group has 40 gen AI ideas. Budget covers three pilots. Which selection approach is the most defensible?
questions.hint: Prioritise by value, feasibility and risk.

options.text: Score ideas on business value, data readiness, feasibility and risk, then pilot a balanced shortlist
options.business_rationale: A structured scoring avoids picking on enthusiasm alone.

options.text: Pick the three ideas championed by the most senior executives, since sponsorship guarantees success
options.business_rationale: Sponsorship helps but doesn't replace feasibility and value checks.

options.text: Pick the three most technically ambitious ideas to show leadership in AI
options.business_rationale: Ambition without readiness or value wastes budget.

options.text: Run all 40 ideas at a tiny scale so no team feels left out
options.business_rationale: Spreading effort thinly delays learning and rarely reaches the value threshold.

questions.scenario_question: A logistics firm's pilot reduced time to draft customs documents by 40%, at a licence and integration cost of 300,000 euros per year. The CFO asks for the business case. Which approach gives the most credible estimate?
questions.hint: Convert time saved into value with real baselines.

options.text: Skip the business case, because strategic projects don't need one
options.business_rationale: Without a case, scaling decisions are guesses.

options.text: Multiply 40% by the whole department's salary budget and call it savings
options.business_rationale: That assumes all time converts to cash and ignores unrelated work.

options.text: Use the vendor's case study from another industry as the estimate
options.business_rationale: Another firm's results don't transfer reliably.

options.text: Measure baseline volumes and time per document, value the hours saved or redeployed, include running and review costs, and test sensitivity
options.business_rationale: Baseline-driven numbers with costs included are credible.

questions.scenario_question: A bank rolled out a drafting assistant, but loan officers barely use it. Interviews show they fear that using it signals they are replaceable, and the tool doesn't fit their workflow. What is the best response?
questions.hint: Adoption is human and workflow-driven.

options.text: Mandate usage with performance penalties for non-use
options.business_rationale: Mandates can deepen resistance.

options.text: Involve officers in redesigning the workflow, communicate how roles evolve, and provide training and champions
options.business_rationale: Addressing fears and fit drives adoption.

options.text: Replace the officers' tool with a more powerful model
options.business_rationale: The barrier isn't capability.

options.text: Cancel the program since people clearly dislike AI
options.business_rationale: Concerns can be addressed.

questions.scenario_question: A clinic group plans a pilot of a gen AI note-drafting tool. Which pilot design best supports a scale decision?
questions.hint: Define success before starting.

options.text: Launch to all clinicians at once to speed learning
options.business_rationale: Too broad to manage risk.

options.text: Run an open-ended trial and decide by general impressions
options.business_rationale: Impressions are biased.

options.text: Set metrics and a baseline, then run a fixed pilot
options.business_rationale: Pre-defined criteria make results interpretable.

options.text: Pilot with only enthusiasts and skip the baseline
options.business_rationale: Enthusiasts overstate benefits; no baseline means no comparison.

questions.scenario_question: A manufacturer needs an internal assistant over maintenance manuals. Options: buy a ready workplace offering, or build a custom solution. Requirements are standard and the IT team is small. What is the soundest recommendation?
questions.hint: Buy for standard needs; build for differentiation.

options.text: Buy or configure a ready offering and spend scarce engineering effort where the company differentiates
options.business_rationale: Standard needs rarely justify custom builds.

options.text: Do nothing until the team triples in size
options.business_rationale: Delay forfeits value.

options.text: Buy the most expensive offering with every optional feature enabled
options.business_rationale: Price and features don't equal fit.

options.text: Build custom, because owning the code is always strategically superior
options.business_rationale: Ownership has a cost; it isn't always better.

questions.scenario_question: A pharma company's gen AI program is stalling: legal, security, compliance and business units each hold different expectations, and nobody owns decisions. What is the most effective step?
questions.hint: Governance and decision rights.

options.text: Allow the loudest team to decide for everyone
options.business_rationale: That ignores risk functions.

options.text: Let each function proceed independently and merge outcomes later
options.business_rationale: That leads to inconsistent controls and rework.

options.text: Pause all AI work indefinitely until all stakeholders agree on everything
options.business_rationale: Perfect agreement is unrealistic.

options.text: A cross-functional group with decision rights
options.business_rationale: Clarity on ownership unblocks progress.

questions.scenario_question: A telecom operator's pilot succeeded with 50 agents. Scaling to 3,000 agents will raise costs, variability in use cases and support needs. What should leadership plan?
questions.hint: Scaling involves more than copying the pilot.

options.text: Simply multiply the pilot's budget by 60 and launch on day one
options.business_rationale: Costs and needs don't scale linearly.

options.text: Keep the pilot at 50 forever to avoid risk
options.business_rationale: That forgoes value.

options.text: Plan for cost modelling, role-specific training, support, monitoring, governance and phased rollout with stage gates
options.business_rationale: Scale brings operational and organisational complexity.

options.text: Hand the rollout to the vendor with no internal ownership
options.business_rationale: Accountability stays internal.

questions.scenario_question: A consulting firm wants to track the health of its gen AI program. Which metric set is the most balanced?
questions.hint: Adoption, quality, risk and business impact.

options.text: Number of licences purchased
options.business_rationale: Spending isn't impact.

options.text: Active use by role, output quality and rework, incidents and escalations, and business outcomes such as turnaround time
options.business_rationale: A balanced set avoids optimising a single number.

options.text: Number of AI-related press mentions
options.business_rationale: Publicity isn't performance.

options.text: Total number of prompts submitted
options.business_rationale: Volume says little about value.

questions.scenario_question: An insurer's leadership says, 'We need ten prompt engineers.' HR asks what capability the organisation actually needs. Which view is more accurate?
questions.hint: AI literacy across roles plus a few specialists.

options.text: No new skills are needed because tools are intuitive
options.business_rationale: Training improves outcomes and safety.

options.text: Only specialist engineers need to understand AI
options.business_rationale: Business users shape use cases and review.

options.text: Hire solely externally and avoid training current staff
options.business_rationale: Internal domain knowledge is essential.

options.text: Broad AI literacy for business users, domain-expert reviewers, and a small core of technical and governance specialists
options.business_rationale: Value comes from many people using AI well.

questions.scenario_question: A media company wants early visible wins from gen AI without major risk. Which candidate is the best fit?
questions.hint: Internal, reviewable, bounded.

options.text: Replacing the legal review of libel risk with a model
options.business_rationale: Legal review needs qualified people.

options.text: Drafting internal meeting summaries and first-pass headline options reviewed by editors
options.business_rationale: Low risk, easy to review, immediate time savings.

options.text: Auto-publishing AI-written investigative articles without editors
options.business_rationale: High reputational and accuracy risk.

options.text: Changing archive records by model suggestion without checks
options.business_rationale: Altering authoritative records is risky.

questions.scenario_question: An energy company is choosing between two gen AI vendors with similar demos. Which due-diligence step adds the most decision value?
questions.hint: Test on your own tasks and review terms.

options.text: Choose whichever has more customers on its website
options.business_rationale: Logos aren't evidence of fit.

options.text: Choose the cheaper licence without checking data terms
options.business_rationale: Data terms and total cost matter.

options.text: Test both on your tasks; compare terms and total cost
options.business_rationale: Real-task testing and terms reveal real differences.

options.text: Choose the vendor with the more polished presentation
options.business_rationale: Polish isn't capability.

questions.scenario_question: A conglomerate's gen AI portfolio has pilots in five units, many overlapping. The CEO wants focus. Which action best improves return on investment?
questions.hint: Consolidate and share.

options.text: Merge overlaps, share components, fund by evidence
options.business_rationale: Reuse and evidence-based funding raise ROI.

options.text: Fund whichever unit lobbies the loudest
options.business_rationale: Politics isn't evidence.

options.text: Cancel every pilot and restart from scratch next year
options.business_rationale: Learning from pilots would be lost.

options.text: Keep all pilots as they are to preserve autonomy
options.business_rationale: Duplication wastes resources.

questions.scenario_question: An HR team wants to use a gen AI tool to help screen job applicants. Which responsible-AI practice is the most important before use?
questions.hint: Fairness testing and human accountability.

options.text: Skip testing because the vendor says the tool is unbiased
options.business_rationale: Vendor assurances don't replace testing in your context.

options.text: Hide from candidates that AI is used so they are not confused
options.business_rationale: Transparency is part of responsible use.

options.text: Let the tool reject applicants automatically to remove human bias
options.business_rationale: Automation can embed bias, and decisions need accountable people.

options.text: Test for biased outcomes across groups, keep humans accountable for decisions, and document how the tool is used
options.business_rationale: Hiring affects people's lives, so fairness and accountability are central.

questions.scenario_question: A bank uses gen AI to draft explanation letters to customers whose loan applications were declined. A regulator asks how the bank ensures transparency. Which response is the most appropriate?
questions.hint: Explain the role of AI and keep decisions accountable.

options.text: Keep the use of AI confidential to protect proprietary methods
options.business_rationale: Concealing it undermines transparency duties.

options.text: Blame the vendor for any inaccurate explanation
options.business_rationale: Accountability stays with the bank.

options.text: Disclose AI assistance where appropriate, ensure reasons given come from the actual decision criteria, and keep a human accountable for each decision
options.business_rationale: Reasons must be accurate and accountable.

options.text: State that the model produces the reasons independently of the decision engine
options.business_rationale: Reasons must reflect the real decision.

questions.scenario_question: A university considers an AI tutor for first-year students. Which pre-launch assessment best reflects responsible AI?
questions.hint: Consider who could be harmed and how.

options.text: Assess risks to students (wrong guidance, bias, over-reliance, privacy), test with diverse users, and set escalation and oversight
options.business_rationale: Impact assessment before launch identifies harms.

options.text: Launch quickly and assess after complaints
options.business_rationale: Harms may already have occurred.

options.text: Assess only the model's accuracy on one benchmark
options.business_rationale: Benchmarks don't capture all harms.

options.text: Assess only whether the tool is cheaper than tutors
options.business_rationale: Cost alone ignores harm.

questions.scenario_question: An insurer's claims assistant recommends denials. A claimant complains and asks who is responsible. What principle should guide the insurer's design?
questions.hint: Humans and the organisation remain accountable.

options.text: The vendor alone is responsible for every outcome
options.business_rationale: The insurer remains accountable.

options.text: Named human owners with appeal routes and records
options.business_rationale: Accountability can't be delegated to a model.

options.text: Nobody is responsible when AI is involved
options.business_rationale: That is unacceptable in regulated decisions.

options.text: The model is responsible because it made the recommendation
options.business_rationale: Models aren't accountable parties.

questions.scenario_question: A bank's credit-marketing assistant shows offers to certain demographic groups far less often. Which action is the most appropriate?
questions.hint: Measure, investigate, mitigate and monitor.

options.text: Ignore it because the model never intended to discriminate
options.business_rationale: Intent isn't required for harm.

options.text: Remove all demographic fields and declare the problem solved
options.business_rationale: Proxies can reproduce bias.

options.text: Switch to a larger model without testing
options.business_rationale: Size doesn't guarantee fairness.

options.text: Measure outcomes across groups, investigate the data and prompts, apply mitigations, and monitor continuously
options.business_rationale: Systematic disparities require structured response.

questions.scenario_question: A brand uses AI-generated images of 'customers' in advertising. Which responsible practice applies?
questions.hint: Don't mislead audiences.

options.text: Skip review since AI images can't offend anyone
options.business_rationale: They can reflect stereotypes.

options.text: Present them as real customers because audiences prefer testimonials
options.business_rationale: That is deceptive.

options.text: Don't pass off synthetic people; follow disclosure rules
options.business_rationale: Truthful advertising applies to AI content.

options.text: Use real people's likenesses without permission if the AI altered them
options.business_rationale: Likeness rights still apply.

questions.scenario_question: A game studio's chat character occasionally produces hateful language when provoked. Which action best reflects responsible AI?
questions.hint: Build safeguards and monitor.

options.text: Add safety filters and policies, red-team the system, monitor in production, and give players a way to report
options.business_rationale: Layered safeguards reduce harm.

options.text: Rely on a disclaimer that the character may say offensive things
options.business_rationale: Disclaimers don't prevent harm.

options.text: Treat it as acceptable because players provoked it
options.business_rationale: Provocation doesn't excuse harm.

options.text: Remove the character's moderation to stay authentic
options.business_rationale: Removing safeguards increases harm.

questions.scenario_question: A conglomerate publishes AI principles but business units ignore them under delivery pressure. What is the best way to make them operational?
questions.hint: Principles need processes.

options.text: Ask each team to interpret principles privately
options.business_rationale: Inconsistent interpretation weakens control.

options.text: Turn principles into reviews, risk tiers and owners
options.business_rationale: Embedding in process makes principles real.

options.text: Make principles optional so that teams can move faster
options.business_rationale: That guarantees non-compliance.

options.text: Publish the principles more prominently on the website
options.business_rationale: Publicity doesn't change behaviour.

questions.scenario_question: A health-tech firm designs a symptom-chat assistant. Which design choice best reflects privacy by design?
questions.hint: Minimise and protect from the start.

options.text: Collect only needed data, apply consent and retention limits, and restrict access, building these into the design from day one
options.business_rationale: Privacy designed in is stronger than added later.

options.text: Share user chats with advertisers to fund the service
options.business_rationale: That conflicts with health privacy.

options.text: Collect all possible data in case it is useful later
options.business_rationale: Over-collection raises risk.

options.text: Add privacy controls after launch when users ask
options.business_rationale: Retrofitting leaves early exposure.

questions.scenario_question: A legal-tech firm sells a contract-risk scoring tool. A client asks why a contract was scored high-risk. What is the best practice?
questions.hint: Give reasons users can check.

options.text: Say that the model is too complex to explain at all
options.business_rationale: Some explanation of drivers is usually possible.

options.text: Show the clauses behind the score; state limits
options.business_rationale: Explanations that can be checked support appropriate reliance.

options.text: Provide only a number and ask clients to trust it
options.business_rationale: Unverifiable output encourages overreliance.

options.text: Refuse client questions to protect the algorithm
options.business_rationale: Clients need to understand output.

questions.scenario_question: A city launches a gen AI assistant for residents. Testing shows weaker answers in some languages and for users with disabilities. What is the right approach?
questions.hint: Equitable access.

options.text: Launch anyway because most residents use the main language
options.business_rationale: That excludes some residents.

options.text: Tell affected residents to use a different service
options.business_rationale: It shifts the burden.

options.text: Test with diverse groups, improve language and accessibility support, and provide alternative channels
options.business_rationale: Public services must serve all residents.

options.text: Stop public service delivery entirely
options.business_rationale: Alternatives and improvements are better.

questions.scenario_question: A regional clinic wants staff to use a gen AI tool to draft letters to patients. Letters would include names and diagnoses. Which step should come first?
questions.hint: Know where the data goes and under what terms.

options.text: Remove patient names but include full diagnoses and addresses
options.business_rationale: Partial removal can still identify patients.

options.text: Use a free consumer chatbot because it is the quickest to start
options.business_rationale: Consumer tools may lack contractual protections for patient data.

options.text: Ask patients to sign a blanket waiver after the letters are sent
options.business_rationale: Consent after processing doesn't fix prior exposure.

options.text: Choose an approved enterprise tool with appropriate data-protection terms, and confirm the lawful basis and access controls
options.business_rationale: Sensitive health data demands approved tools and clear legal footing.

questions.scenario_question: A pharma company connects an assistant to many repositories. Testers show a marketing user can get answers drawn from unpublished trial data. What principle was violated, and what is the fix?
questions.hint: Least privilege and permission-aware retrieval.

options.text: Least privilege: enforce document-level access in retrieval and review which repositories are connected
options.business_rationale: AI should expose only what users are entitled to see.

options.text: Model size: use a smaller model that cannot read trial data
options.business_rationale: Size doesn't control access.

options.text: Data minimisation is irrelevant here, so add disclaimers
options.business_rationale: Disclaimers won't stop disclosure.

options.text: Open access: give everyone equal access to avoid confusion
options.business_rationale: That worsens exposure.

questions.scenario_question: A European public body must keep citizen data within specific regions. It is evaluating a managed gen AI service. Which procurement requirement is most important?
questions.hint: Location of processing and storage.

options.text: An assurance that the vendor is a large company
options.business_rationale: Size isn't a residency assurance.

options.text: Written commitments on regions for processing and storage, plus controls and audit evidence
options.business_rationale: Residency obligations need contractual and technical assurance.

options.text: A promise that data will be handled 'responsibly' without specifics
options.business_rationale: Vague promises don't meet residency rules.

options.text: A friendly user interface in the local language
options.business_rationale: UI language is unrelated.

questions.scenario_question: A law firm wants to use a gen AI service on client documents. The managing partner asks what to confirm about training use of prompts and outputs. What is the best answer?
questions.hint: Read and document the terms.

options.text: Assume all data is used and ban the tool
options.business_rationale: Terms may offer protections that make use acceptable.

options.text: Ask the model whether it will remember the documents
options.business_rationale: The model isn't the authority on contractual data use.

options.text: Assume no data is ever used because AI vendors value privacy
options.business_rationale: Assumptions are not assurances.

options.text: Check the contract on training use; document it
options.business_rationale: Terms vary and must be checked rather than assumed.

questions.scenario_question: An e-commerce company's support chats contain emails and addresses. It wants to analyse them with gen AI to find common issues. Which preparation is most sensible?
questions.hint: Reduce identifiability before analysis.

options.text: Avoid analysis altogether because chats contain personal data
options.business_rationale: Masking enables safe analysis.

options.text: Keep identifiers and publish findings with real customer names
options.business_rationale: That exposes customers.

options.text: Mask identifiers, restrict access, keep a trail
options.business_rationale: Minimising personal data lowers risk.

options.text: Send the raw chats to any external tool for speed
options.business_rationale: Raw personal data raises exposure.

questions.scenario_question: A tech company finds employees pasting confidential designs into public chatbots. The CISO wants a lasting fix. Which package of actions is the most effective?
questions.hint: Provide a safe alternative, set policy, and detect.

options.text: Allow it because productivity gains outweigh leaks
options.business_rationale: Leaks of confidential designs can be costly.

options.text: Block all internet access
options.business_rationale: That harms legitimate work.

options.text: An approved alternative, clear policy and controls
options.business_rationale: Alternatives plus policy plus controls change behaviour.

options.text: Send a warning email once and consider it finished
options.business_rationale: One email rarely changes habits.

questions.scenario_question: A bank logs all prompts and responses of its assistant for audit. The privacy officer worries about storing sensitive customer data indefinitely. What is the best balance?
questions.hint: Audit needs versus data minimisation.

options.text: Stop logging to protect privacy
options.business_rationale: That removes audit ability.

options.text: Log for audit, redact, restrict, set retention
options.business_rationale: Auditability and privacy can both be met.

options.text: Keep all raw logs forever and give broad access to analysts
options.business_rationale: That maximises exposure.

options.text: Log only the model's name
options.business_rationale: Insufficient for audit.

questions.scenario_question: An insurer uses an AI agent from a third-party vendor that connects to claims data. The vendor suffers a breach. What should the insurer have prepared?
questions.hint: Third-party risk management.

options.text: A policy of sending all data to the vendor for convenience
options.business_rationale: That increases exposure.

options.text: Nothing, since the vendor is solely responsible
options.business_rationale: The insurer remains accountable for its data.

options.text: A guarantee that breaches cannot occur
options.business_rationale: No such guarantee exists.

options.text: Due diligence, contractual security and breach-notification terms, data minimisation to the vendor, and an incident response plan
options.business_rationale: Vendors extend the attack surface.

questions.scenario_question: A media company's staff assistant is connected to shared drives. An audit finds many files shared with 'anyone in the company' that should be limited. What matters most before wider rollout?
questions.hint: Clean up over-sharing.

options.text: Review and correct over-shared files and permissions, because the assistant surfaces whatever access allows
options.business_rationale: AI makes over-sharing more discoverable.

options.text: Tell staff not to ask about sensitive subjects
options.business_rationale: Instructions don't enforce access.

options.text: Give the assistant fewer features so that it finds less
options.business_rationale: Feature reduction doesn't fix permissions.

options.text: Wait for a data breach to prioritise cleanup
options.business_rationale: Reactive is costly.

questions.scenario_question: A hospital asks what baseline security controls it should expect from a managed gen AI platform handling clinical data. Which list is the most appropriate?
questions.hint: Core controls.

options.text: Encryption in transit and at rest, identity and access management, audit logging, network controls and compliance certifications relevant to health data
options.business_rationale: These are baseline expectations for sensitive workloads.

options.text: A colourful dashboard and responsive support chat
options.business_rationale: Cosmetic features aren't controls.

options.text: A large library of pre-written prompts
options.business_rationale: Prompts aren't security controls.

options.text: A guarantee that no human will ever see the data
options.business_rationale: Not a realistic or sufficient control.

questions.scenario_question: A consulting firm sets rules for which data may be used with which AI tool. What is the most practical framework?
questions.hint: Classify data, then map to approved tools.

options.text: Ban all AI tools regardless of the data
options.business_rationale: That's disproportionate.

options.text: Allow every tool for every data type
options.business_rationale: Ignores risk differences.

options.text: Classify data in tiers and map each to tools
options.business_rationale: Clear tiers make decisions simple for staff.

options.text: Let each employee decide case by case without guidance
options.business_rationale: Inconsistent decisions lead to leaks.

questions.scenario_question: A CISO tells the board the company will align its AI programme with SAIF, Google's Secure AI Framework. A director asks what SAIF is. Which description is the most accurate?
questions.hint: A conceptual framework for securing AI systems.

options.text: A specific chatbot that answers security questions
options.business_rationale: It's not a chatbot.

options.text: A framework of practices for securing AI systems across their lifecycle, extending established security principles to AI-specific risks
options.business_rationale: It is guidance, not a single product.

options.text: A hardware chip that makes AI models secure by itself
options.business_rationale: SAIF is not a chip.

options.text: A compliance certificate issued automatically to any company that uses cloud AI
options.business_rationale: It isn't an automatic certificate.

questions.scenario_question: A retailer's agent summarises supplier emails and updates purchase orders. A supplier email contains hidden instructions to change bank details. Which control is the most effective?
questions.hint: Limit what untrusted content can cause.

options.text: Give the agent full ERP rights so it can detect fraud itself
options.business_rationale: Excess privilege magnifies damage.

options.text: Trust the model to ignore malicious text on its own
options.business_rationale: Models can be manipulated.

options.text: Disable email reading for all staff
options.business_rationale: Overbroad.

options.text: Treat content as untrusted; approve sensitive changes
options.business_rationale: Layered controls blunt prompt injection.

questions.scenario_question: A bank retrains a fraud-related model weekly on data that includes customer-submitted feedback. A security analyst warns about data poisoning. What is the risk, and what control helps?
questions.hint: Malicious training data.

options.text: The risk is only that customers will dislike the interface
options.business_rationale: Not related.

options.text: Validate training data sources and watch for drift
options.business_rationale: Provenance and validation reduce poisoning risk.

options.text: The model will run out of memory; buy more storage
options.business_rationale: Not the poisoning risk.

options.text: There is no risk because trained models are immutable
options.business_rationale: Retraining pipelines can be poisoned.

questions.scenario_question: A software firm downloads an open model and a set of third-party plug-ins for its AI assistant. Which security practice is the most relevant?
questions.hint: AI supply chain.

options.text: Trust anything with many downloads
options.business_rationale: Popularity isn't safety.

options.text: Avoid version tracking to reduce overhead
options.business_rationale: Versions are needed to patch.

options.text: Vet, test, version and limit plug-ins
options.business_rationale: Supply-chain components can carry vulnerabilities.

options.text: Install everything in production first to see if it works
options.business_rationale: Risky.

questions.scenario_question: An AI assistant generates code and shell commands that engineers paste into production with little review. What risk does this pose, and what is the sound practice?
questions.hint: Treat model output as untrusted input.

options.text: Block engineers from ever using AI
options.business_rationale: Overbroad.

options.text: Let the assistant run commands in production directly
options.business_rationale: That removes safeguards.

options.text: Model output is always safe because the model was trained on good code
options.business_rationale: Training doesn't guarantee safe output.

options.text: Model output can be wrong or unsafe, so review it, test in safe environments and apply the same controls as for any untrusted input
options.business_rationale: Unreviewed execution is risky.

questions.scenario_question: A bank is about to launch a customer-facing assistant. Which pre-launch security activity gives the most insight into real weaknesses?
questions.hint: Adversarial testing.

options.text: Red-team exercises that attempt prompt injection, data extraction and policy bypass, followed by fixes and re-testing
options.business_rationale: Adversarial testing finds issues normal testing misses.

options.text: A friendly demonstration to executives
options.business_rationale: Demos don't probe weaknesses.

options.text: Testing only normal customer questions
options.business_rationale: Misses attacks.

options.text: Waiting for attackers to report problems
options.business_rationale: Reactive.

questions.scenario_question: A telecom operator's assistant is live. The security team asks what to monitor beyond uptime. Which set is the most useful?
questions.hint: Behaviour and abuse signals.

options.text: Unusual prompts, blocked or flagged content, tool-use anomalies, data-access patterns, cost spikes and user reports
options.business_rationale: These signals reveal abuse or failure.

options.text: Only the number of daily users
options.business_rationale: Doesn't show security.

options.text: Nothing beyond uptime since the model is stable
options.business_rationale: Misses abuse.

options.text: Only server temperature
options.business_rationale: Insufficient.

questions.scenario_question: A startup's tuned model is its main intellectual property, exposed through an API. What risks should it consider, and what controls help?
questions.hint: Protect model and API.

options.text: Remove authentication to simplify use
options.business_rationale: Increases risk.

options.text: Model extraction by heavy querying and unauthorised access; use authentication, rate limits, monitoring and access control
options.business_rationale: Controls on the API protect the asset.

options.text: Publish the model weights to deter theft
options.business_rationale: Defeats the purpose.

options.text: None, because models cannot be copied
options.business_rationale: Extraction is possible.

questions.scenario_question: A hospital says, 'Our cloud AI provider is certified, so security is fully their responsibility.' What is the best correction?
questions.hint: Shared responsibility.

options.text: Responsibility belongs to patients
options.business_rationale: No.

options.text: The hospital is right; certified providers cover everything
options.business_rationale: Customers keep responsibilities.

options.text: Certifications are meaningless
options.business_rationale: They are useful evidence.

options.text: Shared responsibility: the hospital secures its use
options.business_rationale: Certification covers the provider's part.

questions.scenario_question: A conglomerate wants to embed security into its AI lifecycle rather than reviewing at the end. Which approach best reflects this?
questions.hint: Security at every stage.

options.text: Skip security reviews for internal pilots
options.business_rationale: Pilots can leak data.

options.text: A single security review the week before launch
options.business_rationale: Too late.

options.text: Security at each lifecycle stage
options.business_rationale: Lifecycle security catches issues earlier.

options.text: Security handled only by the vendor
options.business_rationale: Customer duties remain.

questions.scenario_question: A law firm's associate wants to send an AI-drafted client advisory directly after a quick skim. Which principle applies?
questions.hint: Professional accountability.

options.text: Clients are accountable for checking the advice
options.business_rationale: Clients rely on the firm.

options.text: A qualified person reviews and owns the advice
options.business_rationale: The firm and lawyer remain accountable.

options.text: The AI is accountable once it drafts the text
options.business_rationale: AI cannot hold accountability.

options.text: Review is optional for short documents
options.business_rationale: Short advice can still be wrong.

questions.scenario_question: A bank designs oversight for gen AI uses: email drafting, customer chatbot answers on fees, and credit-limit recommendations. Which approach to oversight is the most sensible?
questions.hint: Scale oversight with risk.

options.text: Match oversight depth to risk
options.business_rationale: Oversight depth should match impact.

options.text: No human oversight for any because AI is accurate
options.business_rationale: High-impact decisions need people.

options.text: Identical heavy review for all three uses
options.business_rationale: Wastes effort and slows low-risk work.

options.text: Human review only for email drafts
options.business_rationale: Reverses the risk logic.

questions.scenario_question: Clinicians using an AI triage assistant accept its suggestions 98% of the time, even in cases where they would have decided differently. What risk is this, and what mitigates it?
questions.hint: Automation bias.

options.text: Model fatigue; give the model rest
options.business_rationale: Models don't tire.

options.text: Good practice; high acceptance means high quality
options.business_rationale: High acceptance can be over-trust.

options.text: Data compression; reduce file sizes
options.business_rationale: Unrelated.

options.text: Automation bias: show evidence; audit overrides
options.business_rationale: Design can counter over-trust.

questions.scenario_question: An airline's agent handles rebooking. In rare cases of unusual routings or distressed passengers, it mishandles requests. How should the airline design human involvement?
questions.hint: Defined escalation triggers.

options.text: Let the agent keep trying until it succeeds
options.business_rationale: Loops frustrate customers.

options.text: Remove humans to avoid delays
options.business_rationale: Humans handle exceptions.

options.text: Define triggers for escalation (low confidence, unusual cases, distress) and pass full context to a human
options.business_rationale: Clear triggers protect customers.

options.text: Escalate every request to a human
options.business_rationale: Defeats the purpose of automation.

questions.scenario_question: An insurer's AI recommends claim outcomes. Auditors ask who decides. Which arrangement is the most defensible?
questions.hint: Humans decide; AI informs.

options.text: Nobody records decisions
options.business_rationale: Auditability required.

options.text: The vendor decides
options.business_rationale: The insurer remains accountable.

options.text: Adjusters decide; the AI informs
options.business_rationale: Accountability sits with named decision-makers.

options.text: The AI decides and adjusters rubber-stamp
options.business_rationale: That blurs accountability.

questions.scenario_question: A government agency uses AI to prioritise inspections. Citizens affected want to challenge decisions. What should the agency provide?
questions.hint: Contestability.

options.text: A chatbot that repeats the decision
options.business_rationale: Not a review.

options.text: A route to human review, with explanations
options.business_rationale: Affected people need a way to contest.

options.text: A statement that the algorithm is confidential
options.business_rationale: Doesn't help challengers.

options.text: No route, as AI decisions are final
options.business_rationale: Removes accountability.

questions.scenario_question: A retailer finds that reviewers approving AI-drafted customer replies often miss subtle errors. What would most improve the oversight?
questions.hint: Effective review needs support.

options.text: Hire reviewers without training
options.business_rationale: Untrained reviewers miss errors.

options.text: Remove reviewers and trust the AI
options.business_rationale: Eliminates the control.

options.text: Tell reviewers to read faster
options.business_rationale: Speed hurts quality.

options.text: Train reviewers on common failure modes, provide checklists and source links, and sample-audit approvals
options.business_rationale: Review quality depends on skill and tooling.

questions.scenario_question: A logistics company plans to give an agent increasing autonomy over time. Which rollout approach reflects good governance?
questions.hint: Earn autonomy with evidence.

options.text: Add autonomy in stages as reliability is shown
options.business_rationale: Autonomy should follow demonstrated reliability.

options.text: Give full autonomy on day one to maximise savings
options.business_rationale: Risky without evidence.

options.text: Never allow any automation
options.business_rationale: Overly restrictive.

options.text: Increase autonomy whenever executives request it
options.business_rationale: Evidence should drive it.

questions.scenario_question: A telecom operator has 25 internal AI assistants, and nobody knows who owns each when problems arise. What is the right remedy?
questions.hint: Named ownership.

options.text: Assign ownership to the vendor
options.business_rationale: Internal accountability remains.

options.text: Let the assistants self-govern
options.business_rationale: Systems can't be accountable.

options.text: Delete the inventory to reduce overhead
options.business_rationale: Inventory is needed.

options.text: Assign a named business owner and technical owner per assistant, with an inventory, review cadence and escalation
options.business_rationale: Ownership enables accountability.

questions.scenario_question: A conglomerate wants a culture where employees feel safe to question AI outputs and report issues. Which measure is the most effective?
questions.hint: Psychological safety and clear channels.

options.text: Rely on external auditors only
options.business_rationale: Internal reporting is faster.

options.text: Provide easy reporting channels, protect people who raise concerns, share learnings and recognise good catches
options.business_rationale: Safe reporting surfaces problems early.

options.text: Keep incidents confidential from other teams
options.business_rationale: Prevents learning.

options.text: Penalise employees who question AI outputs
options.business_rationale: Discourages reporting.
